title: Enhancing Teacher Effectiveness with AI based Prompt Engineering: A Proof of Concept
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI prompt engineering can help teachers create instructional materials more efficiently and with better alignment to standards and classroom goals. The authors frame the work as a proof of concept focused on improving teacher effectiveness, reducing the burden of curriculum creation, and supporting differentiated instruction in K-12 settings, especially middle school STEAM/social studies contexts.

The intervention is a structured prompting framework built around four elements: task context, task input/variable, task instructions, and task criteria. The authors used Microsoft Copilot and demonstrated the process through example prompts for creating simplified informational texts and advanced learning questions aligned to standards, learning targets, and assessment questions. The workflow also emphasized iterative refinement of prompts when outputs were not satisfactory, as well as collaboration among educators to improve prompts.

The paper focuses on middle school teachers in Georgia, with examples drawn from 7th grade social studies and STEAM instruction aligned to Georgia standards and NGSS. The evidence is primarily reflective and descriptive, based on the experiences of two teacher-authors who piloted the process. The main conclusion is that structured prompt engineering can produce higher-quality, standards-aligned instructional materials more consistently, save time, and support differentiated instruction, but it depends on teachers having strong curriculum design knowledge and clear instructional goals.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI/chatbot used for generating and refining text and instructional materials from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the main AI tool in the proof-of-concept prompt engineering workflow; the authors note use of Microsoft Copilot in the implementation and reference ChatGPT/Gemini as examples of LLM tools in the broader discussion.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational AI/chatbot based on large language models for text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned as an example of an LLM tool educators may use; no separate evaluation results reported for Gemini specifically.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model chatbots used for prompt-based content generation and instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper presents a prompt-engineering framework for teachers using generative AI to create informational texts, quizzes, rubrics, differentiated materials, and standards-aligned lesson components.

findings.finding_summary: This proof-of-concept reports that a structured prompt-engineering process helped teachers generate educational materials more quickly and with improved consistency and quality. The authors state that the process enabled production of multiple standards-aligned texts at varying complexity levels and supported differentiated instruction, but no quantitative outcome data, sample size, or statistical effect is reported.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated quality/consistency of AI-generated instructional materials and perceived efficiency of curriculum development

findings.finding_summary: The authors report that the workflow reduced the time and mental effort associated with curriculum development and administrative tasks, freeing teachers to focus more on student interaction. These benefits are described qualitatively in reflections from two teachers; no numerical estimate of time saved is provided.
findings.measure: Perceived efficiency, workload reduction, and ease of curriculum/resource creation

quality_tier_rationale: This is a proof-of-concept / reflective paper with no controlled design, no quantitative outcome analysis, and no inferential statistics. The evidence is qualitative and descriptive, so it does not meet criteria for higher-tier causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful practical benefits for teacher productivity and instructional material quality, but it provides no effect sizes or measured student outcomes. Impact is therefore plausible but empirically unclear.
